AI Research Progress Through the Years · 2025 🚀

AI Research in 2025: The Year Reasoning, Agents and Test-Time Compute Broke Out

2025 was the year the field's focus shifted from building bigger models to making models reason longer, interact, improve themselves and help with discovery. Reinforcement learning produced reasoning. Thinking time became something you could scale. Models wrote their own practice problems. Agents rewrote their own code, and AI started discovering algorithms. This guide covers eighteen papers that set up 2026's self-improving-agent era. They are grouped by the research direction they established rather than ranked. Each gets a plain-English explanation and an animation, followed by what it found, why it matters and its sources.

How to read this: the second article in AI Research Progress Through the Years, and the prequel to AI Research in 2026. Awards come from the official ICLR 2025, ICML 2025 and NeurIPS 2025 announcements; papers without awards were chosen for influence. The "🧒 In plain English" boxes simplify on purpose, and the animations illustrate ideas; exact claims are in "What they found" and the linked papers.

03 🧠 Reasoning and Test-Time Compute

SFT-heavy reasoning → RL reasoning → inference-time scaling → self-generated curricula.

🐋

DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning

DeepSeek-AI · arXiv Jan 2025 · Nature, Sep 2025
📰 Nature📝 Preprint / report
🧒 In plain English

Instead of showing a model thousands of worked solutions, DeepSeek let it practise: it tries maths and coding problems, gets a point when the final answer checks out, and adjusts. With nothing else, the model taught itself to write longer chains of thought, double-check and backtrack — even pausing mid-solution to say, in effect, "wait, let me re-think this" (the paper's "aha moment").

▶ Reasoning learned by practice R1-Zero on AIME 2024, as reported
🔍 What they found
  • R1-Zero: pure RL from a base model raised AIME 2024 pass@1 from 15.6% to 71.0% (86.7% with majority voting)
  • Emergent self-verification, reflection and longer reasoning
  • R1 adds a small cold-start SFT stage and multi-stage post-training for readability
  • Distilled Qwen and Llama models brought reasoning to the open ecosystem; the paper became the first major LLM paper peer-reviewed in Nature
💡 Why it matters

It opened reasoning-model techniques to everyone and made RL the default route to reasoning.

🔗 References
  • DeepSeek-R1 (arXiv 2501.12948)
  • Nature — DeepSeek-R1 incentivizes reasoning in LLMs through reinforcement learning
  • DeepSeek-R1 repository
⏱️

s1: Simple Test-Time Scaling

Muennighoff et al. · arXiv Jan 2025 · EMNLP 2025
📄 Accepted paper
🧒 In plain English

Two simple tricks. First, fine-tune on just 1,000 carefully chosen reasoning examples. Second, control how long the model thinks: stop it when the budget is used up, or — when it tries to stop too early — append the word "Wait" so it keeps checking. More thinking time, better answers.

▶ Budget forcing Drag the thinking budget
🔍 What they found
  • s1-32B (Qwen2.5-32B fine-tuned on s1K) beats o1-preview on competition maths by up to 27% (MATH, AIME24)
  • Budget forcing extrapolates: AIME24 50% → 57%
  • Model, data and code fully open
💡 Why it matters

Made test-time compute an open, reproducible research direction rather than a proprietary secret.

🔗 References
  • s1: Simple test-time scaling (arXiv 2501.19393)
  • EMNLP 2025 — ACL Anthology
♾️

Absolute Zero: Reinforced Self-Play Reasoning with Zero Data

Zhao et al. · arXiv May 2025 · NeurIPS 2025
📄 Accepted paper
🧒 In plain English

What if a model wrote its own homework? One model plays two roles: a proposer that invents coding puzzles just hard enough to learn from, and a solver that tries them. A code executor checks both the puzzles and the answers, so no human data is needed.

▶ Self-play: propose → solve → verify One model, two roles
🔍 What they found
  • Trained with zero external data, the Absolute Zero Reasoner reaches state-of-the-art among zero-setting models on coding and maths
  • Outperforms models trained on tens of thousands of human-curated examples
  • Works across model sizes and families
💡 Why it matters

An early example of a system generating the experiences it learns from — a building block for self-improvement.

🔗 References
  • Absolute Zero (arXiv 2505.03335)
  • NeurIPS 2025 poster
  • Code repository

04 🤝 Agents, Interaction and Early Self-Improvement

From answering one turn well to collaborating, learning from interaction and rewriting one's own code.

🧬

Darwin Gödel Machine

Zhang, Hu, Lu, Lange & Clune · arXiv May 2025 · ICLR 2026
📝 Preprint / report
🧒 In plain English

A coding agent that edits its own code — its tools, prompts and workflow — then tests the new version. Every working variant is kept in a family tree, so later generations can branch from any ancestor, like evolution.

▶ An evolving archive of agents Each dot = one agent version
🔍 What they found
  • SWE-bench 20.0% → 50.0%; Polyglot 14.2% → 30.7%
  • Discovered improvements (better editing tools, context management, peer review) transferred across models
  • Also documented reward hacking — a warning for self-improving systems
💡 Why it matters

One of the clearest bridges from agent engineering to recursive self-improvement.

🔗 References
  • Darwin Gödel Machine (arXiv 2505.22954)
  • Sakana AI — The Darwin Gödel Machine
💬

CollabLLM: From Passive Responders to Active Collaborators

Wu et al. (Stanford, Microsoft) · ICML 2025
🏆 Outstanding Paper
🧒 In plain English

Most chatbots are trained to give the best answer right now. CollabLLM trains them for the whole conversation: it simulates how the chat might continue and rewards replies that lead to a better outcome later — which often means asking a clarifying question first.

▶ Same request, two assistants Pick one
🔍 What they found
  • Multiturn-aware rewards estimated by simulating future conversation turns
  • Better task performance and interactivity; higher user satisfaction and less time spent in a user study
💡 Why it matters

Anticipates 2026's focus on multi-turn reliability (see LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation).

🔗 References
  • CollabLLM (arXiv 2502.00640)
  • ICML 2025 Outstanding Papers
🔁

RAGEN: Self-Evolution in LLM Agents via Multi-Turn RL

Wang et al. · arXiv Apr 2025
📝 Preprint / report
🧒 In plain English

Training an agent over many steps of interaction is unstable. RAGEN found a failure it calls the Echo Trap: the agent finds one pattern that earns some reward and repeats it, its answers stop varying, and learning stalls. Filtering for varied, informative attempts (StarPO-S) keeps it learning.

▶ The Echo Trap Toggle the stabilised version
🔍 What they found
  • StarPO: trajectory-level RL framework for multi-turn agents
  • Echo Trap: reward-variance collapse, entropy drop, gradient spikes
  • Stabilisers: variance-based trajectory filtering, critic baselines, decoupled clipping; diverse initial states help
💡 Why it matters

A bridge from reasoning RL on single answers to agents that learn from environments.

🔗 References
  • RAGEN (arXiv 2504.20073)
  • RAGEN repository

05 🧱 Model Architecture and Attention

Attention architecture → understanding fine-tuning → targeted model editing.

🚪

Gated Attention for Large Language Models

Qwen team (Alibaba) et al. · NeurIPS 2025
🏆 Best Paper
🧒 In plain English

Attention decides how much each word looks at every other word. Models develop a strange habit: they dump lots of attention on the first token (an "attention sink") just to have somewhere to put it. Adding a tiny learned gate after attention lets each head say "nothing useful here" instead — cleaner, more stable and better at long texts.

▶ Where attention goes Toggle the gate
🔍 What they found
  • A head-specific sigmoid gate after scaled dot-product attention, tested across many large-scale runs
  • Better performance, training stability and long-context extrapolation; removes attention-sink behaviour
  • Adopted in Qwen3-Next
💡 Why it matters

Shows the Transformer itself is still improving, not only the systems built around it.

🔗 References
  • NeurIPS Blog — Best Paper Awards 2025
  • Alizila — Qwen wins NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper
🔍

Learning Dynamics of LLM Finetuning

Ren & Sutherland · ICLR 2025
🏆 Outstanding Paper
🧒 In plain English

Fine-tuning is usually treated as a black box. This paper tracks, step by step, how learning one example shifts the model's answers to other examples. It explains odd effects — like preference training (DPO) run too long making even the good answers less likely, because probability gets "squeezed" into one favourite response.

▶ The squeezing effect Drag training steps
🔍 What they found
  • A framework decomposing how each update influences predictions on other inputs
  • Explains hallucination patterns after SFT and the "squeezing effect" in off-policy DPO
  • Suggests simple fixes, e.g. training on rejected responses first
💡 Why it matters

Turns fine-tuning from trial and error into something that can be predicted.

🔗 References
  • Learning Dynamics of LLM Finetuning (arXiv 2407.10490)
  • ICLR Blog — Outstanding Paper Awards 2025
✏️

AlphaEdit: Null-Space Constrained Knowledge Editing

Fang et al. · ICLR 2025
🏆 Outstanding Paper
🧒 In plain English

Suppose a fact changes — a country gets a new leader. Editing the model's weights to learn it often breaks other facts nearby. AlphaEdit only changes the weights in "directions" that the preserved knowledge doesn't use (its null space), so the new fact goes in and everything else stays put.

▶ Edit one fact Compare editing methods
🔍 What they found
  • Projects each edit onto the null space of preserved knowledge before applying it
  • Average 36.7% improvement over the best baseline — by adding one line of code to MEMIT
💡 Why it matters

Precise, controllable updates to what a model knows — important for trustworthy models.

🔗 References
  • AlphaEdit (arXiv 2410.02355)
  • ICLR Blog — Outstanding Paper Awards 2025

06 🌫️ Diffusion and Alternatives to Autoregression

Is next-token prediction the only path forward?

🧩

Train for the Worst, Plan for the Best: Token Ordering in Masked Diffusions

Kim, Shah, Kontonis, Kakade & Chen · ICML 2025
🏆 Outstanding Paper
🧒 In plain English

Masked diffusion models fill in a masked sequence in any order. Training is hard because they must handle every order, including terrible ones. But at inference time you can choose the order: fill in the cells you're most sure of first — like solving a Sudoku by starting with the obvious squares.

▶ Solve a Sudoku row Random order vs most-confident first
🔍 What they found
  • Training on all orders includes computationally hard sub-problems
  • Adaptive, confidence-based decoding needs no retraining: Sudoku accuracy 6.88% → 89.49%, beating autoregressive models trained with the correct order
💡 Why it matters

Shows when flexible ordering is an advantage — the 2025 counterpart to 2026's Flexibility Trap.

🔗 References
  • Train for the Worst, Plan for the Best (arXiv 2502.06768)
  • Kempner Institute — ICML 2025 Outstanding Paper
🖼️

Why Diffusion Models Don't Memorize

NeurIPS 2025
🏆 Best Paper
🧒 In plain English

Big image models could simply memorise their training pictures. Why don't they? Training has two clocks: one when the model starts producing good new images, and a later one when it starts copying training images. The second clock slows down as the dataset grows — leaving a wide window where you stop training with a model that generalises.

▶ Two training clocks Drag the dataset size
🔍 What they found
  • Generalisation time stays roughly constant; memorisation time grows linearly with training-set size
  • Implicit dynamical regularisation in training explains why over-parameterised diffusion models generalise
💡 Why it matters

Theoretical grounding for training generative models that create rather than copy.

🔗 References
  • NeurIPS Blog — Best Paper Awards 2025

07 🛡️ Safety, Reliability and Evaluation

Can models reason? Are they robust? Aligned deeply? Becoming too similar?

🛡️

Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep

Qi et al. · ICLR 2025
🏆 Outstanding Paper
🧒 In plain English

A safety-trained model mostly learns to start its answer with "I can't help with that." The paper shows the safety lives almost entirely in those first few words. Trick the model past them — by pre-filling "Sure, here's how…" — and it happily continues. The fix: train it to recover and refuse later in the answer too.

▶ How deep is the safety? Try a prefilling attack
🔍 What they found
  • Alignment mostly changes the distribution of the first few output tokens
  • Explains prefilling attacks, some jailbreaks and fine-tuning attacks
  • Remedies: data augmentation with recovery examples; a token-wise constrained fine-tuning objective protecting early tokens
💡 Why it matters

A simple, unifying explanation for many jailbreaks — and a direction for deeper alignment.

🔗 References
  • Qi et al. — Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep (arXiv 2406.05946)
  • ICLR Blog — Outstanding Paper Awards 2025
🗼

The Illusion of Thinking

Shojaee et al. (Apple) · NeurIPS 2025
📄 Accepted paper
🧒 In plain English

Instead of benchmarks that may have leaked into training, the authors used puzzles with a difficulty dial, like Tower of Hanoi with more and more disks. Reasoning models beat ordinary ones at medium difficulty — but past a point, accuracy collapses, and strangely they start thinking less, not more.

▶ Tower of Hanoi difficulty dial Drag the number of disks
🔍 What they found
  • Three regimes: standard models win at low complexity, reasoning models at medium, both collapse at high
  • Reasoning effort rises with complexity, then declines despite spare token budget
  • Contested: follow-up work argued some failures reflect output-length limits and evaluation choices
💡 Why it matters

Pushed evaluation from final-answer accuracy to how reasoning behaves as problems scale.

🔗 References
  • The Illusion of Thinking (arXiv 2506.06941)
  • Apple Machine Learning Research
  • Response: Thinking Isn't an Illusion (arXiv 2507.17699)
🐝

Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models

Jiang et al. (UW, AI2 et al.) · NeurIPS 2025 Datasets & Benchmarks
🏆 Best Paper
🧒 In plain English

Ask 70 different AI models to "write a metaphor about time" and you'd expect 70 different ideas. Instead most say nearly the same thing ("time is a river…"). Each model repeats itself, and different models from different companies converge on the same answers.

▶ "Write a metaphor about time" Many models, few ideas
🔍 What they found
  • Infinity-Chat: 26K real-world open-ended queries with 31K dense human annotations
  • Strong intra-model repetition and inter-model convergence across 70+ LLMs
  • Reward models and LLM judges are poorly calibrated to diverse human preferences
💡 Why it matters

Raises concerns about diversity, homogenisation of human thought and preference optimisation.

🔗 References
  • Artificial Hivemind — NeurIPS 2025 proceedings
  • Allen School — NeurIPS Best Paper for Artificial Hivemind

08 🔬 AI Doing R&D

AI → experiment → objective feedback → improved algorithm → next experiment.

🧪

AlphaEvolve: A Coding Agent for Scientific and Algorithmic Discovery

Google DeepMind · May 2025 (white paper, arXiv Jun 2025)
📝 Preprint / report
🧒 In plain English

Gemini writes many candidate programs; automatic tests score each one; the best are kept and mutated again — evolution for code. Because every program is scored objectively, it can discover genuinely new algorithms, including ones that speed up the training of the very model that runs it.

▶ Generate → evaluate → evolve Real reported results appear as it runs
🔍 What they found
  • 4×4 complex matrix multiplication with 48 scalar multiplications, improving on Strassen's 1969 result
  • Data-centre scheduling heuristic recovering ~0.7% of Google's stranded compute
  • 23% faster Gemini matrix-multiplication kernel → ~1% less Gemini training time; hardware-design and FlashAttention improvements
💡 Why it matters

The clearest 2025 precursor to AI improving the process that builds AI.

🔗 References
  • AlphaEvolve (arXiv 2506.13131)
  • Google DeepMind — AlphaEvolve
📄

The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Discovery

Sakana AI · arXiv Apr 2025
📝 Preprint / report
🧒 In plain English

An AI that does the whole research job: comes up with an idea, designs and runs experiments by exploring a tree of options, analyses results, draws figures and writes the paper. One of its fully AI-written papers scored above the acceptance threshold at an ICLR workshop.

▶ From idea to paper Press play
🔍 What they found
  • Agentic tree search over experiments; vision-language feedback on figures
  • 3 papers submitted to an ICLR 2025 workshop; 1 averaged 6.33 — above the acceptance threshold (withdrawn by agreement)
  • System later published in Nature (March 2026)
💡 Why it matters

Foreshadowed 2026's automated-R&D wave (see AI Doing R&D).

🔗 References
  • The AI Scientist-v2 (arXiv 2504.08066)
  • Code repository

09 🤖 Reinforcement Learning Beyond LLMs

The scaling story isn't unique to language models.

🦿

1000 Layer Networks for Self-Supervised RL

Wang et al. · NeurIPS 2025
🏆 Best Paper
🧒 In plain English

Reinforcement-learning agents usually use shallow networks (2–5 layers). Here a robot learns to reach goals with no reward and no demonstrations, and the authors made its network up to about 1,000 layers deep. Deeper networks unlocked new skills — walking and manipulating far better.

▶ Deeper networks, new skills Drag network depth
🔍 What they found
  • Scaled self-supervised (contrastive) goal-conditioned RL networks to 1,024 layers
  • 2× to 50× performance gains on locomotion and manipulation; qualitatively new behaviours emerge with depth
💡 Why it matters

Suggests the scaling story isn't unique to language models.

🔗 References
  • NeurIPS Blog — Best Paper Awards 2025

10 👁️ Multimodal Foundation Models

Foundation-model ideas spreading from language into vision and video.

🎯

SAM 2: Segment Anything in Images and Videos

Ravi et al. (Meta FAIR) · ICLR 2025
🏅 Honorable Mention
🧒 In plain English

Click on an object once, and SAM 2 outlines it — in a photo, and then frame after frame through a video, even when it moves or is briefly hidden, thanks to a memory of what it has seen.

▶ Click once, track through video Press play
🔍 What they found
  • Unified promptable segmentation for images and video with a streaming memory
  • Real-time video segmentation; large SA-V video dataset released
💡 Why it matters

Foundation-model ideas extending from language into persistent visual understanding.

🔗 References
  • SAM 2 (arXiv 2408.00714)
  • ICLR Blog — Outstanding Paper Awards 2025

11 Test-Time Compute, Simulated

Two 2025 papers pull in opposite directions. s1 says more thinking helps; The Illusion of Thinking says reasoning collapses on hard enough problems. A toy model shows both can be true at once. Extra "Wait" re-checks catch errors while the problem fits the thinking budget, and nothing helps once it doesn't:

▶ Accuracy vs problem length Same model as the script below
"""Test-time compute in a toy model: why "think longer" helps - until it doesn't.

A problem needs n reasoning steps; each step is wrong with probability 3%. The model has a budget of
160 step-tokens. After finishing, it may say "Wait" k times (s1-style budget forcing): each re-check
costs n/2 tokens and finds and fixes one remaining error with probability 60%. If the solution plus
re-checks do not fit in the budget, the model runs out and fails - a crude stand-in for the accuracy
collapse on very complex puzzles reported in "The Illusion of Thinking". Illustrative, stdlib only.
"""
import random

def solve(n, k, rng, err=0.03, budget=160, fix=0.6):
    if n + k * n / 2 > budget: k = max(0, int((budget - n) // (n / 2)))   # use only the re-checks that fit
    if n > budget: return False
    errors = sum(rng.random() < err for _ in range(n))
    for _ in range(k):
        if errors and rng.random() < fix: errors -= 1
    return errors == 0

def acc(n, k, trials=20000):
    rng = random.Random(n * 100 + k)
    return sum(solve(n, k, rng) for _ in range(trials)) / trials

print("Accuracy for a 30-step problem as the model is told to 'Wait' and re-check k times")
for k in [0, 1, 2, 4, 8]:
    print(f"   k={k}:  {acc(30, k):.1%}")
print("\nAccuracy as problems get longer (budget 160 step-tokens)")
print(f"   {'steps':>5} {'no re-check':>12} {'up to 4 re-checks':>18}")
for n in [10, 30, 60, 100, 150, 200]:
    print(f"   {n:>5} {acc(n, 0):>12.1%} {acc(n, 4):>18.1%}")
print("\nExtra thinking fixes errors on problems that fit the budget; past it, accuracy collapses.")

Output:

Accuracy for a 30-step problem as the model is told to 'Wait' and re-check k times
   k=0:  40.1%
   k=1:  61.9%
   k=2:  77.1%
   k=4:  92.8%
   k=8:  99.2%

Accuracy as problems get longer (budget 160 step-tokens)
   steps  no re-check  up to 4 re-checks
      10        73.8%              98.6%
      30        40.1%              92.8%
      60        16.2%              65.7%
     100         4.6%              13.7%
     150         1.1%               1.0%
     200         0.0%               0.0%

Extra thinking fixes errors on problems that fit the budget; past it, accuracy collapses.

13 Key Takeaways from 2025

✅ RL can produce strong reasoning behaviour.
✅ Inference-time compute can be explicitly scaled.
✅ Models can generate their own learning problems.
✅ Agents can modify their own scaffolding.
✅ LLMs can take part in algorithmic and scientific discovery.
✅ Verification, safety and evaluation became central.

A counterpoint worth knowing: a NeurIPS 2025 runner-up, Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?, found that RL with verifiable rewards mostly makes a model more reliable at reasoning it could already sometimes do, rather than creating genuinely new abilities. The debate over whether RL teaches or sharpens continues. It is covered in the RSI series' Data vs Reinforcement Learning.

AI research in 2025, in one paragraph
2025 was the transition year from "scale the model" to "scale reasoning and interaction". DeepSeek-R1 showed reinforcement learning can produce reasoning, s1 showed thinking time can be scaled cheaply and openly, and Absolute Zero showed a model can write its own curriculum. Agents became collaborators (CollabLLM), learners from interaction (RAGEN) and self-modifiers (the Darwin Gödel Machine). AlphaEvolve and The AI Scientist-v2 put AI inside the discovery loop. The Transformer itself still improved (gated attention), fine-tuning and editing became more predictable, and diffusion models were better understood. Meanwhile, papers on shallow safety, reasoning collapse and homogeneous outputs made verification and evaluation central. Those threads — self-generated learning, self-modifying agents, automated discovery and verification — are exactly what 2026 built on.
